Start the design now and you're digging when the ground thaws. Start in spring and you're fighting snow on your foundation next fall.

posts.caption:
How long does a commercial buildout take? The construction is usually the short part.

Design and drawings come first. Then the city reviews them for a permit, and that review can take weeks or months depending on the jurisdiction and how busy they are. Then pricing, ordering, and lead times on things like HVAC units and storefront glass. Then construction, inspections, and the certificate of occupancy.

Owners get burned when they plan around the construction time and forget the rest. Count from the day you start design, not the day we show up with tools.

posts.caption:
What it takes to keep a job moving through a Colorado winter.

Poly enclosures around the work so trades can keep going. Temporary heat so mud, paint, and concrete cure right. A snow removal plan so the first storm doesn't shut the site for three days. Ground thaw blankets so footings don't go in on frozen dirt.

None of it is free, and it should be in the budget from day one, not a surprise change order in January.

Building this winter? Save this and ask your contractor where winter conditions are in the price.

Three bids, three numbers, and the low one looks great. Before you sign, check these:

Exclusions. What did they leave out? Permits, utility fees, and dumpsters are common.
Allowances. A low allowance for fixtures or flooring makes a bid look cheap and bills you later.
Schedule. A bid with no schedule is a guess.
General conditions. Supervision, cleanup, and temporary facilities have to be somewhere.
Assumptions. Read every one.

Line them up apples to apples and the low bid is often not the low bid.

Send this to whoever is collecting your bids.

How the low bid turns into the expensive bid.

It excluded the permit. It carried a fixture allowance that wouldn't buy half the fixtures. It assumed the existing panel was good. It left out winter conditions. Each one shows up later as a change order, after you've already signed.

The bid that reads more expensive up front often just told you the truth. Read the exclusions page first. It's the most honest page in the document.

Front Range soil moves. A lot of Northern Colorado sits on clay and claystone that swells when it gets wet and shrinks when it dries, and that movement cracks slabs, racks doors, and breaks plumbing.

The geotechnical report is how you find out what you're building on. It drives the foundation: footings, drilled piers, over-excavation, structural floors, or a combination. Skip it and you're guessing with the most expensive part of the building.

If a contractor prices your foundation without asking for a soils report, ask why.

posts.caption:
GMP stands for Guaranteed Maximum Price, and on design-build work it's one of the most common ways to contract.

The contractor builds the job at actual cost plus an agreed fee, up to a cap. If the job runs over the cap without a change in scope, the contractor eats it. If it comes in under, the savings go back to the owner, or get split, depending on the contract.

What makes it work: open books. You should be able to see what was spent and why.

Save this for your next contract meeting.

How a building gets put on the ground.

The surveyor sets control points. We set batter boards and string lines off those points, check the corners, check the diagonals, and check them again. Then the excavator digs to the strings.

A quarter inch off at layout becomes a wall that doesn't line up, a door that doesn't fit, or a building over the setback line. That's why the superintendent is standing out there with a tape in the cold at 6 AM.

Turning an office into a gym, a warehouse into a brewery, or a retail space into a clinic? Changing how a building is used can trigger code upgrades the old tenant never had to make.

The usual ones: fire sprinklers or alarms, more exits, accessible restrooms and routes, ventilation, and sometimes structural work for heavier loads.

On top of that, the ADA can require up to 20 percent of your alteration budget to go toward the accessible route to the space you changed.

Find out before you buy or sign, not at plan review.

No contingency is a plan to run out of money.

Every project finds something. A buried footing nobody knew about. Rotten framing behind finished walls. A city comment that adds work. A finish you change your mind on.

Carry a contingency of your own, separate from the contractor's, sized to how much you don't know. Older building, more unknowns, bigger contingency. If you don't use it, great. If you need it and don't have it, the job stops.

Building in Steamboat means designing for snow, and a lot of it.

The roof structure has to carry snow loads many times what Loveland designs for. Roof shape decides where snow slides, and nobody wants it sliding onto an entry, a walkway, a deck, or the neighbor's lot. Snow storage on the site has to be planned, not improvised. Deliveries get harder once winter sets in.

Those decisions belong in the design. Fixing them after the first big winter means tearing into a finished building.

Your construction schedule has hundreds of lines. One path through it matters most: the critical path.

The critical path is the chain of tasks where any delay pushes your finish date. Pouring the foundation, then framing, then the roof, then inspections, and so on. Other tasks have float, meaning they can slip without hurting the end date.

Ask your contractor to show you the critical path and what's on it this week. If they can't, nobody is managing the date.

posts.caption:
Colorado's energy code changed on July 1, 2026. The state's model low energy and carbon code became the minimum, and any city or county that updates its building codes now has to adopt it or something stronger.

What it means for new buildings: solar-ready, electric-ready, and EV-ready. Heating, cooling, water heating, and lighting must be able to cut load when the utility asks. For homes, the bigger the house, the stricter it gets, and homes 7,500 square feet and up have to be net-zero energy.

Which code applies depends on your jurisdiction and when it last updated. Check before you design, not after.

Save this. Send it to anyone designing a new building in Colorado.

When a budget comes in high, cut finishes, not the envelope.

Finishes can be upgraded later: flooring, fixtures, paint, lighting trim. The roof, insulation, windows, and air barrier are built once and live with the building for decades. Cheap there shows up as leaks, condensation, ice, and an energy bill you pay every month.

Good value engineering asks what each dollar does over the life of the building, not just what it does on bid day.

Pre-engineered metal buildings are one of the fastest ways to get a shop, warehouse, ag building, or equipment barn standing in Northern Colorado.

What makes them work: the frame and panels are engineered and cut for your building, so erection goes fast. Clear spans are long, so you get open floor space.

What people miss: the building package is only part of the cost. Foundation, slab, utilities, insulation, doors, and the permit are on top. And the building has to be designed for the snow and wind loads where it's going.

Who pulls the building permit, you or the contractor?

On commercial work, the licensed general contractor pulls it. That puts the contractor's name, license, and insurance on the line with the city, which is how it should be. Some jurisdictions let property owners pull permits for their own homes, but then the owner owns every inspection and every code problem.

If a contractor asks you to pull the permit in your name, ask why they won't.

The difference is in the planning, long before the first wall.

posts.caption:
Design-build or design-bid-build: which costs less?

Design-bid-build gets you a hard bid on finished drawings, which feels safe. But the drawings were done without a builder pricing them, so redesign after bids is common, and the gap between drawings and field shows up as change orders.

Design-build prices the job while it's being designed, starts long-lead buying earlier, and puts one firm on the hook for both.

The cheaper method is the one that gets you the building you need on the date you need it with the fewest surprises.

Save this for your next project kickoff.

posts.caption:
How owners end up paying twice for the same work: the contractor gets paid, a sub or supplier doesn't, and that sub files a mechanic's lien on your property.

The protection is lien waivers. With every payment, get waivers from the contractor and from the subs and suppliers they paid with your last payment. Conditional waivers cover the payment being made now. Unconditional waivers confirm the money cleared.

It's paperwork. It's also the difference between a closed job and a lien on your building.

Save this. Send it to whoever approves your contractor's invoices.

Many Colorado cities license contractors by type, and the license has to match the work. The certificate of insurance should come from the insurance agent, show general liability and workers' comp, and name you as additional insured on commercial work. Call the agent to confirm it's current.

Ask anyone you hire what license and certifications they hold, then check them.

The construction is done, the furniture is in, and you still can't open. You're waiting on the certificate of occupancy.

The CO is the building department's sign-off that the space is safe to use for what you said you'd use it for. It comes after the final inspections: building, fire, electrical, plumbing, mechanical, and sometimes health and zoning. Some jurisdictions issue a temporary CO while small items finish.

posts.caption:
What's retainage? It's a percentage the owner holds back from each payment to the contractor until the job is finished.

It exists to give the owner leverage at the end: the punch list gets done, the closeout paperwork shows up, and the last subs get paid. The contract sets the percentage, when it can be reduced, and when it's released. Public projects have their own rules set by law.

Used right, retainage keeps everyone finishing strong. Used as a weapon, it starves subs who did their work. The contract should say clearly how it comes back.

Save this for your next contract review.

Slabs, decks, and roofs get checked so snow doesn't load something that isn't ready for it. Exterior work moves to the next good day. Interior work keeps going if the building is closed and heated.

A good schedule already has snow days in it. Northern Colorado guarantees them.

The fees nobody put in the budget.

New buildings and some expansions pay for their connection to city water, sewer, and power, and some jurisdictions add impact fees for roads, parks, or schools. On commercial work they can run five figures or more, and bigger meters cost more.

They're due before you can get service, so they hit early. Ask the city for a fee estimate during design, not after the permit.

Save this. Ask your jurisdiction for a fee estimate.

Does the building have enough power for what you're going to do in it? Find out before you sign.

Commercial kitchens, manufacturing equipment, EV chargers, and big HVAC loads can outrun an existing service. Upgrading means engineering, coordination with the utility, and equipment that can take many months to arrive. In Loveland that's Loveland Water and Power, and the utility side runs on its own timeline.

Get the load calculated early. Power is often the long pole in the tent.

posts.caption:
Once this slab is poured, every pipe under it is buried for the life of the building.

So before concrete, the under-slab plumbing gets laid to slope, supported, and tested. Drain lines are filled with water or put under pressure and held so any leak shows up now, and the inspector signs off before anything gets covered. Sleeves go in where pipes pass through the slab so the concrete doesn't grab them.

A leak found today is a fitting. A leak found next year is a jackhammer.

Follow for what happens before the concrete truck shows up.
